title: 5 Best Penetrating Concrete Sealers (2026): Nothing to Peel
h1: The 5 Best Penetrating Concrete Sealers in 2026
description: Foundation Armor SX5000 tops 5 penetrating concrete sealers; premium silane-siloxane repellents are often rated for 5 to 10 years on exterior concrete.

intro: Penetrating sealers work inside the concrete, so there is nothing on top to peel, scuff or yellow. The catch is that the word covers several different chemistries, and they do different jobs.

A penetrating sealer is the closest thing concrete has to an invisible raincoat that cannot wear off. It soaks in, reacts, and leaves the surface looking and feeling exactly as it did. That is also why it is easy to buy the wrong one: a silicate densifier and a silane water repellent look identical in the pail, yet one hardens concrete and the other keeps water out. This guide sorts the best penetrating sealers by what they actually do.
quickAnswer: the Foundation Armor SX5000 Silane-Siloxane is our #1 pick (best overall). The penetrating sealer that suits the widest range of concrete and masonry with the fewest compromises.

Eagle Natural Seal is a good illustration of the gap between budget and premium penetrating sealers. It is a water-based repellent that does the core job: water beads, the slab looks unchanged, and nothing on the surface can peel. It is easy to buy locally, simple to roll or spray, and cleans up with water. What you give up is depth and duration. Budget repellents typically carry less active material, so they penetrate less and wear out sooner, and owners commonly report reapplying after a few seasons on heavily exposed concrete. That is not a deal breaker. On a covered porch, a garden path or a patio in a mild climate, a shorter cycle at a lower price can make sense. On a salted driveway or a north-facing wall that stays damp, the premium silane-siloxanes above are worth the extra money because each application lasts considerably longer.

Below-grade concrete needs a different kind of penetrating sealer. The water problem in a basement comes from outside the wall or below the floor, and moisture moving through concrete will blister any film applied to the inside face. RadonSeal Plus is a deep-penetrating silicate formulation that reacts with the lime in concrete to form crystalline deposits in the capillaries, tightening the material from within. The company markets it for reducing dampness, efflorescence and radon entry and describes the result as permanent, since nothing remains on the surface to wear. It is not a leak stopper. Running water at a crack or the wall-floor joint needs injection repair or drainage work. Paint, old sealers and efflorescence must come off first, because the product has to reach bare concrete. For a musty basement with chalky walls and a damp-feeling slab, it is one of the more direct DIY treatments available.

Consolideck LS is here because many people shopping for a penetrating sealer actually need a densifier. Concrete is full of tiny capillary pores that wick water in from the surface. A film-forming sealer covers those pores with a layer of acrylic, urethane or epoxy. A penetrating sealer goes into them instead. The liquid soaks a few millimeters into the slab, and the active ingredient either lines the pore walls with a water-repellent layer or reacts with the cement chemistry to partly fill and tighten them.

Because the treatment lives below the surface, there is nothing to wear, peel or delaminate. Tires, shovels and foot traffic contact the concrete itself, not a coating. That is the main reason penetrating sealers dominate on driveways, bridges and parking structures, where film coatings wear out in a few seasons.

Water repellents in this group also leave the concrete breathable. Water vapor can still move out through the pores, but liquid water and dissolved salt are pushed back. That matters for slabs on grade and for masonry walls, where trapping moisture behind a film causes blistering, peeling and, in cold climates, freeze damage behind the coating.

The trade-off is that you see little or nothing. Most penetrating sealers dry clear and matte, with no color enhancement. If you want concrete to look richer or glossier, you need a film, as covered in our [guide to choosing a concrete sealer](/best-concrete-sealer/), or a penetrating product specifically sold as color-enhancing.

sections.h: Silane, Siloxane, Silicate and Siliconate Compared

blocks.p: **Silanes** are the smallest molecules in the family, which lets them reach deeper into dense concrete. They react with moisture in the presence of the slab's alkalinity to form a durable water-repellent lining. High-solids silanes are what transportation agencies typically specify for bridge decks and highway concrete exposed to salt.

**Siloxanes** are larger, partly reacted molecules. They do not penetrate dense concrete as deeply, but they bridge the larger pores of brick, block and porous stone and tend to bead water strongly at the surface. Most consumer products blend silane and siloxane to cover both cases. Our [silane vs. siloxane breakdown](/silane-vs-siloxane-sealers/) explains when the ratio matters.

**Silicates**, in sodium, potassium or lithium form, are densifiers rather than water repellents. They react with calcium hydroxide to form extra binder, hardening the surface and reducing dusting and porosity. **Siliconates** are older water-repellent chemistry, usually potassium or sodium methyl siliconate, often used on porous masonry and as an economical treatment; they react with carbon dioxide in air to form a repellent layer.

sections.h: Active Solids and Carrier: Reading the Label

blocks.p: Two numbers explain most of the price difference between penetrating sealers. The first is active content, often given as percent solids or percent silane-siloxane. A product with 20 to 40 percent active material carries more repellent into the concrete per gallon than one with a few percent. Commercial bridge-deck silanes can run far higher. Budget products often do not state the figure at all, which is itself a clue.

Higher active content generally means deeper penetration and longer service life, but it is not the only factor. Molecule size, carrier, and how well the product is applied all matter. A modest-solids product applied generously in two passes can outperform a high-solids one that was sprayed on lightly and left with dry gaps.

The second number is the carrier. Water-borne sealers are low odor, safer to use near living spaces, and clean up with water. Solvent-borne sealers can penetrate dense concrete a little more readily and tolerate cooler application conditions, but they have strong odors, flammability concerns and, in some states, VOC restrictions. For homeowners, water-borne is the sensible default unless the label of a solvent product solves a specific problem.

Concentrates add a third consideration. A jug that dilutes several times with water may look expensive, but the cost per finished gallon can be lower than ready-to-use products. The flip side is that mixing becomes your responsibility. Measure carefully, mix completely, and do not stretch the ratio to cover more ground.

sections.h: Matching the Sealer to the Surface

blocks.p: Dense, smooth, trowel-finished concrete, such as a garage floor or an interior slab, is hard for any penetrating product to enter. Silane-heavy repellents and lithium densifiers do best here. Before buying, try the water drop test: if water sits on the surface without darkening it after several minutes, the concrete may already be sealed or too dense for a repellent to absorb, and you should investigate before spending money.

Broom-finished exterior concrete, the typical driveway and walkway, absorbs readily and suits any good silane-siloxane blend. For driveway-specific picks and salt considerations, see our [concrete driveway sealer reviews](/best-concrete-driveway-sealer-reviews/).

Porous masonry, including brick, split-face block and some natural stone, often does better with siloxane-rich products that bridge larger pores. These surfaces also tend to be vertical, which makes run-down a concern; apply from the bottom up in light passes so the sealer does not sheet off before soaking in. For walls specifically, our [brick sealer guide](/best-brick-sealer-reviews/) and [cinder block sealer guide](/best-cinder-block-sealer-reviews/) go further.

Pavers sit between concrete and masonry. Many penetrating sealers are labeled for them, but paver owners often want joint stabilization or color enhancement, which penetrating repellents do not provide. If that is your goal, look at a dedicated [paver sealer](/best-paver-sealer/) instead.

They do not stop oil. Silane-siloxane repellents are designed around water and dissolved salts. Motor oil and grease are attracted to the same treated surface, so drips still stain, although often more shallowly. A few products advertise added oil repellency, but for a garage floor where stains matter, a coating is the dependable answer.

They do not fill cracks or stop running water. A penetrating sealer will reduce dampness through sound concrete, but water entering through a crack, a cold joint or a failed foundation drain needs a crack repair or drainage fix. Treat the source first, then seal the concrete around it.

They do not repair damage. Scaling, spalling and pitting are permanent losses of surface material. Sealing a damaged slab slows further deterioration but does not restore the surface. If appearance matters, a resurfacing product may be needed before sealing.

And they do not change appearance much, which can disappoint people expecting a fresh look. If the concrete is stained, mildewed or faded, clean it first and accept that a penetrating sealer will preserve it as is. For a darker or glossier finish, a film or an enhancing product is required.

sections.h: Applying a Penetrating Sealer the Right Way

blocks.p: Start with clean, dry, bare concrete. Pressure wash to remove dirt and mildew, degrease oil spots, and remove any old film sealer, paint or efflorescence. Then let the slab dry at least a day, longer in cool or shaded areas. Penetrating products cannot soak into pores that are already full of water.

A low-pressure pump sprayer is the usual tool. Many labels call for a flood coat: enough product that the surface stays wet for a short time, then a second pass applied wet-on-wet before the first dries. Others call for two separate coats. Follow your product's instructions precisely, because the timing changes how deeply it penetrates.

Watch for puddles in low spots. Standing sealer that dries on the surface can leave a shiny or blotchy residue. Back-roll or broom puddles out while the surface is still wet. On vertical surfaces, spray from the bottom up so runs fall onto areas already treated.

Work within the temperature and weather window on the label, commonly around 40 or 50 to 90 degrees Fahrenheit, with no rain expected for at least half a day to a full day. Keep pets and people off until dry, and protect plants, glass and nearby painted surfaces from overspray. Our [driveway sealing walkthrough](/how-to-seal-a-concrete-driveway/) covers the full sequence step by step.

Because penetrating sealers are invisible, the water test is your proof. A day or two after curing, sprinkle water across the treated area. Water should bead or sit on the surface without darkening the concrete. Any spot that darkens quickly was missed or under-applied and should get another pass.

Do the test in several places, especially along edges, in low spots, and where you changed sprayer tanks. Gaps tend to appear in predictable spots: the end of each pass, around obstacles, and under overhangs where you could not see well.

Over the years, repeat the test each fall. Repellency fades gradually, usually first in tire paths and other high-wear areas. When water starts soaking in within a minute or two, reapply to those areas. You rarely need to redo an entire slab at once.

Densifier then repellent is the most common layering approach, and it works well on old, dusty exterior concrete. Apply the silicate first, let it react for the time stated on the label, then apply the silane-siloxane once the slab is dry. Many manufacturers publish instructions for exactly this combination.

A film over a repellent is trickier. Silane-siloxane treatment is designed to keep liquids out, which includes water-based acrylics. Some products allow a topcoat after the repellent has cured or weathered, but adhesion can suffer. If you might want a wet look later, check both labels or start with the film instead.

Plan ahead for paint, epoxy and flooring. Silicone-based repellents can interfere with adhesion of paint and coatings, while silicate densifiers usually do not. If a basement floor or garage may get an epoxy, tile or vinyl floor later, use a densifier or a compatible primer system rather than a water repellent.

Finally, keep records. Note the product, date and coverage. Penetrating sealers leave no visible trace, so the next owner, or you in ten years, will have no way to tell what is on the slab without testing. That note makes future decisions easy.
Also Needed for This Job

mistakes: Buying a densifier for water problems

Silicate densifiers harden concrete but repel water only modestly. If your goal is keeping salt and water out of a driveway or wall, you need a silane, siloxane or blend. Use a densifier when the problem is a soft, dusty surface, and pair it with a repellent outdoors.

A penetrating sealer cannot reach concrete through acrylic, urethane or paint. It will sit on the film, dry to a residue and do nothing. Test with water first; if it beads, find out what is on the slab and strip it before using a penetrating product.

Pores full of water cannot absorb sealer. Applying too soon after washing or rain leaves the treatment shallow and short-lived. Give the slab at least a full dry day, longer in shade or cool weather, and check that the surface color is uniform before starting.

Standing sealer in low spots can dry into a shiny, blotchy or sticky patch, especially with high-solids products. Keep a roller or broom handy and work puddles into the surrounding concrete while the surface is still wet.

Because penetrating sealers dry invisible, missed strips are common. A day after application, sprinkle water across the slab and look for areas that darken. Retreat those spots right away rather than finding them after the first winter.
bottomLine: For most exterior concrete and masonry, a water-borne silane-siloxane blend is the right penetrating sealer, and Foundation Armor SX5000 is the most versatile choice. For large salted areas, the Ghostshield 8500 concentrate gives the best cost per square foot, and Eagle Natural Seal is a sound budget option on a shorter cycle. When the problem is a damp basement or a dusty interior floor, a silicate is the better tool: RadonSeal Plus for below-grade concrete and Consolideck LS for interior slabs. Whatever you choose, start with clean, dry, bare concrete, apply generously within the label's window, and confirm the result with a water test.

faqs.q: How deep does a penetrating concrete sealer go?
faqs.a: It depends on the product, the concrete and the application. Labels and technical sheets commonly describe penetration in the range of a few millimeters, with small-molecule silanes reaching deepest into dense concrete. Porous, older concrete absorbs more. Even shallow penetration provides protection, because the damaging freeze-thaw action happens mainly in the top layer.

faqs.q: Do penetrating sealers make concrete waterproof?
faqs.a: No. They make it water-repellent, which greatly reduces how much water and salt soak in from the surface, but they do not stop water under pressure or water entering through cracks. For a basement with active leaks, address cracks and drainage first. Penetrating sealers are about reducing absorption, not creating a waterproof barrier.

faqs.q: Can I use a penetrating sealer on pavers?
faqs.a: Yes, many silane-siloxane products are labeled for pavers, and they protect without changing the color. They do not stabilize joint sand or enhance the color, which many paver owners want. If you need those, use a dedicated paver sealer. Always check that the pavers are clean and free of efflorescence before sealing.

faqs.q: How long does a penetrating sealer last?
faqs.a: Premium silane-siloxane repellents are commonly rated for roughly five to ten years on exterior concrete, depending on exposure and active content. Budget repellents usually last less. Silicate densifiers react permanently, but their water-repelling contribution is limited. Use a water drop test each fall rather than relying on the claimed lifespan.

faqs.q: Will a penetrating sealer stop spalling?
faqs.a: It can reduce the risk of new spalling and scaling by keeping water and salt out of the surface, which limits freeze-thaw damage. It will not repair spalls that already exist. If spalling is caused by corroding rebar or poor concrete, sealing slows the process but does not stop it entirely.

faqs.q: Can I paint over a penetrating sealer?
faqs.a: It depends on the type. Silicate densifiers generally leave concrete receptive to many coatings. Silane and siloxane repellents can interfere with adhesion of paint, epoxy and adhesives because they repel water-based products. If you plan to coat or paint later, check both product labels or choose a densifier instead.

faqs.q: Is a penetrating sealer safe indoors?
faqs.a: Water-borne penetrating sealers and silicate densifiers are commonly used indoors and have low odor. Solvent-borne products should be used only with strong ventilation, and some are labeled for exterior use only. Follow the safety data sheet, ventilate well, and keep children and pets away until the treatment is dry.
